section.title: Area under a graph
section.p: When velocity is nonnegative, distance traveled is the area under the velocity graph. That observation is too useful to keep only for motion.
Given a nonnegative function f on an interval [a,b], we want to measure the area between the graph and the x-axis.

For a curved graph, the height changes. The central idea is to replace the curved region by many thin rectangles.
As the rectangles become thinner, the approximation should improve.

subsection.p: Because x^2 is increasing on [0,2], every left endpoint rectangle lies below the curve on its interval. So this estimate is too small.
If we use right endpoints, the rectangles lie above the curve. That estimate will be too large.
This gives a useful strategy:
subsection.md: \text{trap the unknown area between a lower estimate and an upper estimate.}

exercise.title: Why do thin rectangles make a curved region measurable?

statement.p: Area of a rectangle is height times width. A curved region does not have one height. In your own words, why does replacing the region by many thin rectangles turn an unknown area into a sum we can compute, and why should thinner rectangles be better?

hint.p: On a narrow strip the height hardly changes, so one sample height is a fair representative. The curved area is the limit of those rectangular sums.

exercise.title: Why do left, right, and midpoint sums differ before the limit?

statement.p: Each rule chooses a different height on the same subinterval. In your own words, why can those choices systematically overestimate or underestimate a monotone graph, and why is that disagreement a feature of finite estimates rather than a contradiction?

hint.p: They are three attempts to recover one area from incomplete height information. For an increasing function, left rectangles sit below the graph and right rectangles sit above it.

subsection.title: Upper and lower sums
subsection.p: Left and right rectangles are easy to compute, but they are not always upper or lower estimates. If a function decreases, the left rectangles lie above the curve and the right rectangles lie below it. If a function rises and falls, both can be mixed.
A more reliable idea is to use the largest and smallest function values on each small interval.
On a subinterval, define:
subsection.md: \text{lower height}=\text{smallest value of }f\text{ on that subinterval},
\text{upper height}=\text{largest value of }f\text{ on that subinterval}.

Adding all the lower rectangle areas gives a lower sum. Adding all the upper rectangle areas gives an upper sum.
For a continuous function, the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees that each small closed interval really has a largest and smallest value. This is one reason the theorems about continuity matter.

note.title: The squeezing idea for area
note.p: If upper sums and lower sums can be made as close as we want, then there is only one reasonable number for the area between them.

subsection.p: This is the geometric ancestor of the definite integral.

exercise.title: Why do upper and lower sums squeeze toward a single area?

statement.p: A lower sum uses the smallest height on each piece; an upper sum uses the largest. In your own words, why does forcing those two estimates together leave only one reasonable number for the area between them, and why is that the geometric ancestor of the definite integral?

hint.p: If upper sums and lower sums can be made as close as we want, there is no room left for two different areas.

subsection.title: Area as a limiting process
subsection.p: A curved area is not found by one rectangle. It is found by a limiting process.
This sentence is not yet a formal definition. The formal definition will come after we develop better notation. But the idea is already clear:
subsection.md: \text{thin rectangles make the curved region measurable.}

subsection.p: For y=x, geometry already knew the answer. Rectangles confirmed it.
For y=x^2, geometry does not give such an immediate answer. Rectangles become the method itself. Later, the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus will give a fast way to compute the same area exactly.
For now, the main point is this:
subsection.md: \text{Area under a graph is an accumulation of thin rectangular pieces.}
subsection.p: There is one caution. Not every wild function behaves well enough for this process. If a function jumps too violently at every scale, upper and lower sums may refuse to come together. Continuous functions do behave well, and we will return to that fact later.

To define the integral cleanly, we need a compact language for finite sums. That is where sigma notation enters.

exercise.title: Why is a curved area a limiting process rather than a single rectangle?

statement.p: One rectangle is too crude for a changing height. In your own words, why is the sentence area is the limit of rectangular sums as the widths go to zero already the idea of the integral, even before the formal notation arrives?

hint.p: Thin rectangles make the curved region measurable. The later definition will name that limit; it will not change the idea.
